name: Tundra
notes: Arctic lowland tundra: treeless, permafrost, dominated by mosses, lichens, sedges, dwarf willows and heath shrubs. Drawn on Alaska/Canada, Siberia and Scandinavian Arctic.

shrub.name: Arctic willow
shrub.source: Salix arctica, circumpolar high Arctic, prostrate creeping willow to ~0.5 m, northernmost woody plant

traits.native_range: Salix arctica, circumpolar high Arctic, prostrate creeping willow to ~0
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

shrub.silhouette: prostrate woody mat hugging the ground, catkins upright

growth.juvenile_note: Tiny seedling with 2 round cotyledons and a few silky-haired leaves. Grows only mm to a few cm a year as thick, knobbly trailing stems pressed to the ground and rooting as they go, with broad oval leaves (silky when young, reddish in autumn). Takes decades to make a flat mat; big upright catkins stand above it.
growth.source: Wikipedia/Flora of N America Salix arctica (usually 15 cm tall, a plant in E Greenland dated 236 yr, extremely slow growth); USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual Salix (flowers July, fruit Aug-Sept; seed germinates within 1-2 days); size-age curve and first seed estimated

fruiting.source: USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual Salix table (S. arctica flowers July, ripens Aug-Sept); Flora of N America (large erect female catkins 2-6 cm, reddish, hairy capsules); Arctic willows pollinated by flies and bumblebees plus wind; fruit set, crop and rot estimated (slow decay in cold soils)

shrub.name: Crowberry
shrub.source: Empetrum nigrum, circumboreal heath, evergreen mat shrub 10-30 cm with black berries

traits.native_range: Empetrum nigrum, circumboreal heath, evergreen mat shrub 10-30 cm with black berries
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

shrub.silhouette: dark heath mat of needle-fine twigs

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings are rare: the seed needs winter chilling and germinates poorly. The seedling is a few thin, wiry stems clothed in tiny, glossy, needle-like leaves with rolled-under edges, like a miniature heath. Stems creep and root, spreading 7-15 cm a year into a low, dense, dark-green evergreen mat studded with black berries.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Empetrum nigrum (flowers from snowmelt through July; drupe dark-blue to black with 6-9 nutlets, ripe Aug-late fall, persists through winter under snow; few viable seeds, high seedling mortality, spreads mostly vegetatively; 20-30 yr to recover after fire); Wikipedia (stems grow 7-15 cm/yr, clonal mats)

fruiting.source: Wikipedia (flowers 3-6 mm, greenish-pink sepals turning reddish-purple, May-June; pollinated by generalist insects and wind; fruit 4-6 mm, black, ~7.8 seeds, persists through winter; edible, eaten fresh or in jams); USDA FEIS (ripe Aug-late fall). Fruit set and crop estimated.

shrub.name: Dwarf birch
shrub.source: Betula nana, circumpolar Arctic/subarctic shrub tundra, 0.2-1.2 m, wet peaty ground; leaves turn red in autumn

traits.native_range: Betula nana, circumpolar Arctic/subarctic shrub tundra, 0
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

shrub.silhouette: low tangled shrub of tiny round leaves

growth.juvenile_note: Tiny winged nutlets blow across the snow and sprout in early summer on bare, moist peat or moss. The seedling has two minute oval cotyledons, then small, round, deeply round-toothed leaves on a thin reddish stem; it stays a tiny sprig for years, then branches low and layers into a knee-high spreading mat of wiry brown twigs with coin-sized crinkly leaves that turn red in autumn.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Betula nana (0.15-1 m, slow-growing seedlings, establishment from seed rare, layering and sprouting; 15 d stratification then germination within 14 d at 12 C); Wikipedia (low shade tolerance); growth, first seed and stem ages estimated.

fruiting.source: USDA FEIS (monoecious, wind-pollinated, self-incompatible; female catkins in flower early June; male catkins 10-25 mm, female 6-10 mm; seeds ripen in August and disperse from late summer to the next spring, blowing over snow); Wikipedia (fruiting catkins 5-15 mm); counts are catkins, estimated.

shrub.name: Net-leaved willow
shrub.source: Salix reticulata, circumpolar Arctic-alpine calcareous ground, prostrate rounded net-veined leaves

traits.native_range: Salix reticulata, circumpolar Arctic-alpine calcareous ground, prostrate rounded net-veined leaves
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

shrub.silhouette: ground-hugging mat of round net-veined leaves

growth.juvenile_note: Seedling minute with two round cotyledons; first leaves small, round and dark green. Stems creep on or just under the ground and root, forming a flat mat; each short shoot carries 2-4 round, leathery leaves with a deeply sunken net of veins (whitish below) and, later, slender long-stalked catkins standing upright above the mat.
growth.source: Wikipedia/Flora of N America Salix reticulata (to 8 cm tall, exposed stems to 20 cm, mats 30 cm+ broad; slender yellow catkins tipped pink in spring); USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual Salix (fast germination); spread rate, first seed and lifespan estimated for an arctic-alpine dwarf shrub

fruiting.source: Wikipedia/Flora of N America Salix reticulata (slender long-stalked catkins after the leaves, yellow tipped pink, females reddish; hairy capsules); insect plus wind pollination as in other arctic willows; ripening, set and crop estimated

ground.name: Reindeer lichen

growth.juvenile_note: No seedling: a new patch starts from a broken-off fragment (trampled or carried by wind and reindeer) or, rarely, from spores that must meet a green alga. The young thallus is a scatter of tiny grey stalks that branch in threes and fours, tips all bending one way; over decades they build a springy ash-grey mat up to ~10 cm deep, dying at the base while growing at the tips.
growth.source: Wikipedia Cladonia rangiferina (grows 3-11 mm/yr, 3.9-4.4 mm/yr in Finland; mats to ~10 cm, ~12 cm in humid, 4-6 cm in dry sites; can establish ~2 yr after fire but takes decades to recover; individual lives ~20-30 yr; faster growth in shadier forests)

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; needs a wet film to reproduce, so spread reads moisture not pollinators

ground.source: Tundra and open taiga; grey-white mats the caribou dig for in winter; grows millimetres a year. Index Fungorum.

traits.leaf_shape: tiny leaves packed in a dome
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

leaf.notes: pale grey-white densely branched shrubby tufts, branches curved to one side, in spongy mats

appearance.silhouette: grey-white spongy mats among dwarf shrubs
appearance.refs: Wikipedia Cladonia rangiferina, Brodo Lichens of North America

ground.name: Rusty bog-moss
ground.source: Sphagnum fuscum, circumpolar hummock-forming peat moss in tundra and bogs, brown-green cushions

traits.native_range: Sphagnum fuscum, circumpolar hummock-forming peat moss in tundra and bogs, brown-green cushions
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

ground.silhouette: brown-green moss hummock, soft and rounded

growth.juvenile_note: A spore germinates into a tiny flat green plate (thalloid protonema) that buds leafy shoots within weeks to months. The young colony is a small, very dense cushion of rusty-brown to reddish, tightly packed capitula that grows 0.7-2 cm taller a year and slowly builds a firm hummock; hummocks can be centuries old.
growth.source: Bengtsson et al. 2016 Ecol. Evol. (PMC4833502): S. fuscum length growth 7-20 mm/yr; Heck et al. 2020 bioRxiv (Sphagnum spores form protonemal filaments after 2-20 weeks); hummock-building and sporophyte timing estimated

ground.name: Stair-step moss

growth.juvenile_note: Young plants are small loose wefts of red-stemmed, feathery, olive to golden-green fronds creeping over humus, logs or rock. Each year a new frond arches up from the middle of last year's, so a shoot becomes a staircase of flat, fern-like steps, one per year, the oldest dying brown underneath. A deep carpet rebuilds only slowly after fire, once a canopy has closed.
growth.source: Trees for Life (new segment each year from the centre of the previous one, segments live up to ~8 yr, sporophytes uncommon, slow recolonisation after fire, shade-loving); Wikipedia (one step per year used to age shoots). Lifespan is for the patch; spore-to-plant time and first capsule age estimated.

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; needs a wet film to reproduce, so spread reads moisture not pollinators

ground.source: Boreal and temperate rainforest; one storey per year, so its age is readable. Kew POWO.

traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

leaf.notes: glossy green fern-like fronds in annual tiers; each year's growth a new storey; red-brown stems

appearance.silhouette: layered glossy green carpet in old forest
appearance.refs: Wikipedia, British Bryological Society field guide

ground.name: Lava moss

growth.juvenile_note: Mostly starts from broken shoot fragments (sporophytes are rare): a small tuft of wiry shoots whose narrow leaves end in long, toothed, white hair-points, so the patch looks hoary grey when dry and olive-green when wet. Shoots branch and creep outward, piling up into a springy, woolly carpet 5-15 cm deep over lava, boulders and heath; lower parts die brown.
growth.source: Wikipedia Racomitrium lanuginosum (stems to 12 cm; leaves 3-5 mm with toothed white hair-points; sporophytes rarely produced; capsules 1-1.7 mm); growth (roughly 0.5-1.5 cm of shoot a year) and carpet age estimated from bryological knowledge of Icelandic lava fields and upland heaths

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; needs a wet film to reproduce, so spread reads moisture not pollinators

ground.source: Iceland's lava fields and every cold rock; grey woolly mats that hide the ground. Kew POWO.

ground.name: Tufted hairgrass
ground.source: Deschampsia cespitosa, tufted hairgrass, tussock of wet meadows around cooled hot spring outflows, Holarctic, 0.3-1.2 m — Wikipedia / USDA

traits.native_range: Deschampsia cespitosa, tufted hairgrass, tussock of wet meadows around cooled hot spring outflows, Holarctic, 0
traits.leaf_shape: narrow grass blades in a dense tussock
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

ground.silhouette: dense green tussock with airy seed haze

growth.juvenile_note: Seedling: a small tuft of fine, dark-green, ribbed, rough-edged leaves. It tillers into a dense, fountain-like tussock, flowering from its second year: a cloud of tall, airy, silvery-purple to golden panicles held well above the leaf mound; the tussock base grows wider and denser each year.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Deschampsia cespitosa (densely cespitose, culms 20-120 cm; 95% germination over 30 d with light after cold storage; no seed in the planting year, seed in the second; flowers May-Sep by region; rarely in dense shade; seed viability 1-80% by year). Tussock lifespan estimated.

ground.name: Common cottongrass

growth.juvenile_note: A seedling is a small tuft of narrow, channelled, grass-like leaves on wet peat or mud. It soon sends out long creeping rhizomes, so the plant becomes a loose sward of single shoots rather than a tussock; from its second or third summer each flowering stem carries 3-7 drooping spikelets that burst into white cotton tufts.
growth.source: Flora of North America Eriophorum angustifolium (rhizomatous, not tussock-forming; culms 20-70 cm; 3-7 nodding spikelets; bristles bright white, to 4 cm). Germination, first flowering and clone age estimated.

ground.source: Eriophorum angustifolium, common cottongrass: circumboreal wet tundra, fens and thaw-pond margins; a creeping sedge 20-60 cm with 3-7 nodding white cotton heads per stem. Kew POWO; Flora of North America; Walker et al. 2005 CAVM (wet sedge tundra).

traits.native_range: circumboreal wet tundra, fens and thaw-pond margins
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

leaf.notes: long narrow channelled leaves tapering to a three-sided tip; tips redden early

appearance.seasonal: green in summer; white cotton heads June-August; leaves turn red-brown in autumn
appearance.silhouette: loose sward of thin stems with nodding white cotton tufts
appearance.refs: Flora of North America; Wikipedia Eriophorum angustifolium

ground.name: Arctic bluegrass

growth.juvenile_note: A seedling is a few soft, flat, bright green blades with the boat-shaped tips of all bluegrasses. It tillers and runs by short rhizomes into a loose, low tuft or small sod; flowering stems rise 10-40 cm with an open, pyramid-shaped panicle of purple-tinged spikelets.
growth.source: Flora of North America Poa arctica (loosely tufted to sod-forming, rhizomatous; culms 10-40 cm; panicle open, pyramidal; spikelets often purplish). Germination, first flowering and lifespan estimated.

ground.source: Poa arctica, arctic bluegrass: circumpolar arctic tundra and alpine meadows, moist to mesic ground; loosely tufted, rhizomatous, culms 10-40 cm with an open purplish panicle. Kew POWO; Flora of North America.

ground.name: Polar grass

growth.juvenile_note: A seedling is a small tuft of comparatively broad, flat, bright green leaves. Creeping rhizomes spread it into loose patches; flowering stems rise 20-80 cm with a narrow to spreading panicle of small, purplish-brown, one-flowered spikelets. It is one of the first grasses to colonise disturbed wet tundra.
growth.source: Flora of North America Arctagrostis latifolia (rhizomatous; culms 20-100 cm; leaves flat, 4-10 mm wide; panicle purplish; wet tundra, disturbed ground). Germination, first flowering and lifespan estimated.

ground.source: Arctagrostis latifolia, polar grass: circumpolar wet and moist tundra, sedge meadows and disturbed ground; rhizomatous, culms 20-80 cm, broad flat leaves and a purplish panicle. Kew POWO; Flora of North America.

ground.name: Arctic peat moss

growth.juvenile_note: A spore germinates into a tiny flat green plate that buds leafy shoots; most new colonies start from broken shoot fragments. The shoots end in a flat-topped head (capitulum) of short crowded branches that turns golden to dark brown in the open, and the colony builds low brown hummocks a few millimetres a year in wet tundra fens.
growth.source: Flora of North America Sphagnum arcticum (moderately robust; flat-topped capitulum golden brown, brown or dark brown; low hummocks in weakly to moderately minerotrophic fens; all collections north of 59 N in wet or moist tundra). Growth rate and ages estimated from arctic Sphagnum.

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; needs a wet film to reproduce, so spread reads moisture not pollinators

ground.source: Sphagnum arcticum Flatberg & Frisvoll, arctic peat moss: circumpolar wet and moist tundra (Alaska, Yukon, Quebec, Svalbard, arctic Russia), low dark-brown hummocks in minerotrophic fens. Flora of North America; Flatberg & Frisvoll 1984.

ground.name: Iceland moss

growth.juvenile_note: No seedling: new tufts grow from broken lobes carried by wind, water and grazing reindeer. A young thallus is a few small, erect, channelled brown lobes; over years they lengthen and fork into a loose tuft of stiff, ribbon-like, olive- to chestnut-brown lobes with tiny spines along the edges, growing a few millimetres a year among dwarf shrubs.
growth.source: Brodo, Sharnoff & Sharnoff 2001 Lichens of North America (Cetraria islandica: erect, channelled lobes 3-10 cm, brown, margins with short spinules, white pseudocyphellae beneath); growth a few mm per year as in other tundra mat lichens; ages estimated.

repro.note: a lichen: spreads mainly by broken lobes (trampling, grazing, wind); no flowers

ground.source: Cetraria islandica, Iceland moss (a lichen, not a moss): circumboreal heath, tundra and alpine grassland; tufts of erect, channelled, olive- to chestnut-brown lobes 3-10 cm with spiny margins among dwarf shrubs; reindeer forage. Brodo et al. 2001; Index Fungorum.

ground.name: Tundra puffball

repro.note: The mycelium is the organism and lives in the substrate for years; the mushroom is a days-long fruiting body. 'rhizome' here = the mycelium spreading through the soil or litter; 'wind' = spores.

ground.source: Lycoperdon cretaceum Berk. (syn. Calvatia cretacea), arctic puffball: circumpolar arctic-alpine, most frequent in the Arctic with scattered records in the Alps and Rockies; small chalk-white puffballs on bare soil, among moss and dwarf shrubs in tundra and fellfield. Index Fungorum; Larsson & Jeppson 2008; IUCN Red List (Lycoperdon cretaceum).
